text:
Artichoke, Globe.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Globe artichoke is a large, handsome thistle-family perennial grown for its unopened flower buds, unlike the underground tubers harvested from Jerusalem or Chinese artichokes. It is decorative enough for a border, with grey-green fern-like leaves and strong stems, but it needs more space than most vegetables and is not a natural choice for a very small garden. The reward is a distinctive, fine-flavoured crop: pick the heads while they are still tight and tender, before the scales open and the centre becomes tough. The plants establish quickly in rich, moist but well-drained soil, though they need regular watering, feeding, mulching and some protection in cold winters.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jul – Sep

Seed depth

3/4 in.

Row spacing

36 in. between rows

Yield per mature plant

10-12 heads

Plant spacing

36 in. between plants

Sow

Under cover late Feb–Mar, outdoors in spring.

Plant offsets

Apr. In mild districts, autumn is also possible.

Ready in

First main crop in the second summer after planting

Plant out

Seed-raised plants about Jun, after hardening off.

Recommended varieties
Green Globe

A familiar green-headed artichoke for a permanent sunny bed. Harvest the flower buds while their scales remain tightly closed.

Gros Vert De Laon

A hardy, traditional green artichoke with substantial heads. A sensible alternative for a permanent vegetable garden.

Imperial Star

A seed-grown selection producing generous green heads. A useful addition for gardeners establishing an artichoke bed from seed.

Purple Globe

Purple-tinted heads add colour to the plot and kitchen. Choose for variety alongside a dependable green-headed selection.

Key risks
Aphid

Blackfly and greenfly may gather on developing globe-artichoke flower heads.

Slugs and snails

Young shoots are vulnerable to slugs and snails, which can shelter among old leaves.

Frost damage

Hard frost may cut leaves down, with regrowth appearing in spring.

Botrytis

Grey mould can affect leaves and stalks in damp, stagnant conditions.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
10
STALKS & SHOOTS

Allow room for a large perennial.

Choose a sunny, sheltered position with rich soil and good drainage.

Cut heads before the scales open.

Tight, tender buds give the best kitchen harvest.

Soil & preparation
Sun, shelter and rich, moist, well-drained soil. Improve clay; avoid winter waterlogging.
Work compost or well-rotted manure deeply into soil. Mulch.
Sowing & planting
Position the offset
Firm at the same level
Plant offsets 

Take a rooted side shoot from a productive plant, leaving enough shoots on the parent. Trim the leaf tips and set the crown at its old soil level. Firm and water thoroughly.

From seed 

Sow in pots under cover or in the final bed, ¾ in. deep. Harden off pot-grown plants before setting them out. Offsets give a more dependable crop.

Looking after the crop
Water deeply while plants establish and heads form. Mulch, weed and feed organically after the first heads.
After cropping, clear woody stems and yellow leaves. Keep 3–4 strong new shoots at 8–12 in. high. Replace ageing crowns gradually in spring with suckers from productive plants.
In cold areas protect crowns with loose straw or leaves. Loosen covers in mild wet weather to prevent stagnant damp.
Harvesting & storage
Cut heads while the scales are tight. Very young heads can be eaten almost whole. On older heads eat the heart and fleshy scale bases.
Cut the main head with a short stalk, then smaller side heads as they develop. A long, mild season may give a second flush.
Remove buds in the first summer to build strong roots. Begin harvesting in the second summer.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Aphid	Blackfly or greenfly on young heads.	Squash damaging colonies, encourage predators and cut infested tips.
Slugs and snails	Young shoots and leaves are chewed.	Inspect and hand-pick; clear decaying leaves around crowns.
Frost damage	Hard frost cuts down foliage.	Protect crowns loosely; prevent winter waterlogging.
Botrytis	Grey mould on leaves or stalks.	Remove infected tissue; improve airflow and avoid wet crowns.
Artichoke leaf spot	Spreading brown leaf patches.	Remove badly affected foliage; keep plants open and vigorous.
Mice	Sown seed disappears before germinating.	Raise seed in protected pots or modules where needed.
Final tips

Seed-raised plants vary; offsets from good plants are more dependable.

Replace ageing crowns gradually with vigorous suckers.

Eat very young heads almost whole; use scale bases and hearts of older ones.

Check winter protection after rain; keep crowns clear of stagnant damp.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
11
STALKS & SHOOTS
